html:
A great revolt of slaves in Sicily against the Roman Republic, from 135 to 132 BCE.

Sicily was full of large estates worked by slaves bought from Rome's wars in the east. They were badly fed and often chained. The revolt began at Enna, in the middle of the island, led by Eunus, a Syrian slave who claimed to be a prophet and was said to breathe fire. He took the royal name Antiochus. A second leader, Cleon from Cilicia, took Agrigentum on the south coast and joined him.

The rebels beat several Roman forces and held much of the island. Only in 132 BCE did the consul Publius Rupilius retake Tauromenium and Enna by siege. Eunus was captured and died in prison.

The war showed the danger of Rome's new slave economy, the kind of estate described in Cato's book on farming. Sicily rose again in the Second Servile War of 104 to 100 BCE, and the third and largest revolt was led by Spartacus in Italy itself (see Spartacus' slave revolt). The same years saw the land reforms of Tiberius Gracchus, who worried that slaves were replacing free farmers.
sum: A great revolt of slaves in Sicily against the Roman Republic, from 135 to 132 BCE.
